titleStmt.title: Exact schedulability analysis of systems based on multi-rate periodic cyclic executives

analytic.title: Exact schedulability analysis of systems based on multi-rate periodic cyclic executives

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In a recent survey of industry practitioners in the field of real-time systems, the majority of the respondents indicated that cyclic executives are (still) in use in their systems. Unfortunately, contemporary text books hardly address cyclic executives, if at all. There is therefore a need for analysis techniques for these executives.

In this paper, we consider the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive, scheduling a given sequence of independent hard realtime polling tasks in a single-processor system. We present exact analysis for this cyclic executive, and discuss its relative strengths and weaknesses compared to multi-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead. Unlike existing approaches, which typically take periodic tasks as a starting point for cyclic executives and focus on schedulability of tasks, we take the schedulability of the system as a starting point, i.e. whether or not the system meets its deadlines. In particular, we do not assume periods and deadlines for tasks, and our analysis derives feasible cycle times of a multirate periodic cyclic executive for a system.

div.head: A. Background and motivation
div.p: In a recent survey of 120 industry practitioners in the field of real-time embedded systems [1], it was observed that from the 97 respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in the considered systems, 54.17% answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered". The academic interest in cyclic executives has gradually decreased over the last two decades, however, since it was concluded by C. Douglass Locke [2] that the fixed-priority approach generally dominates the cyclic executive approach for hard real-time systems. As a result, cyclic executives are mentioned in contemporary text books, such as [3]- [6], but hardly addressed in detail. Because cyclic executives are still in use in practice, proper explanation of cyclic executives and their exact analysis remains desirable, however. In earlier work, we therefore presented exact analysis for (basic) multi-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives [7]. This paper presents exact analysis for multi-rate periodic cyclic executives, and discusses its relative strengths and weaknesses compared to multi-rate AFAP and multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead.

div.head: B. Problem description
div.p: Hard real-time systems require timely responses to events. As illustrated by an air bag, a system response (the inflation of an airbag) shall be provided in a well-defined interval relative to the occurrence of an event (a collision), i.e. neither too early nor too late. A system specification may therefore constrain the time-interval from an event to a response by both a lower bound, a so-called best-case system deadline, as well as an upper bound, a so-called worst-case system deadline. For hard real-time computing systems, where control is realized in software, these system deadlines give rise to timing constraints on the real-time tasks that have to detect events (through regularly polling sensors) and provide responses (using actuators).

In this paper, we assume a hard real-time system with a set of n (input) events, a set of n (output) responses, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Events are sporadic, i.e. are characterized by a minimal inter-arrival time.

We assume a single-processor system and a basic multirate cyclic executive to schedule the set of tasks. In particular, we assume a statically known sequence of tasks executed in a continuous loop, in which every task occurs at least once. Although tasks scheduled by means of a cyclic executive are typically assumed to be periodic [8], i.e. are typically assumed to be activated with a fixed inter-arrival time (or period), we do not make that assumption in this paper. The problem addressed in this paper is (i) how to determine the schedulability of the system, i.e. whether or not the best-case and worst-case deadlines of the system are met, and (ii) which multi-rate cyclic executive to choose.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: In this paper, we present exact analysis for multi-rate periodic cyclic executives, assuming that the sequence of jobs to be executed in a cycle is known. In addition, we discuss the relative strengths and weaknesses of the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive compared to the multi-rate AFAP and multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead.

div.head: D. Organization
div.p: The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we present a basic real-time system model. Section III provides a recap of the three basic multi-rate cyclic executives considered. Exact worst-case analysis of the multirate periodic cyclic executive is the topic of Section IV. A discussion on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the cyclic executives can be found in Section V. Options to lift the restrictions of the (basic) multi-rate periodic cyclic executive are discussed in Section VI. We conclude the paper in Section VII. II. A BASIC REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODEL We assume a system S, a set E S of n sporadic (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Each event e i is characterized by a minimal interarrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple e i , r i is characterized by a best-case system deadline BD S i and a worst-case system deadline WD S i , where 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . Moreover, we assume a set T S of n independent polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , where task τ i senses event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i is characterized by a best-case computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , where 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The execution of a task is termed a job. A job of task τ i is denoted by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k, i.e. the first job of τ i is denoted by ι i,0 . The computation time C i,k of every job ι i,k of task τ i shall be between BC i and WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: We assume that tasks are scheduled by cyclic executives, run non-preemptively and do not suspend themselves. The sequence of tasks executed in a cycle is assumed to be known statically. Moreover, we ignore scheduling overhead and system initialization. When a system S meets all its deadlines under a specific cyclic executive and a specific sequence of tasks, the system S is called schedulable under that cyclic executive and that sequence. We use m i ≥ 1 to denote the number of times task τ i is executed in a cycle. For ease of presentation, we assume a sequence int task[] of length N = 1≤i≤n m i representing the cycle for multirate cyclic executives, where the index ranges from 0 to N -1, and a function int idx(job) yielding the index in the sequence of the job job past as an argument, where idx(ι i,k ) = idx(ι i,(k mod mi) ) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and 0 ≤ k. The relation between the sequence int task[] and function int idx(job) is expressed by
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∀ 0≤k<mi task[idx(ι i,k )] = i and ∀ 0≤j≤N -1 ∃! 0≤k<m task[j]
div.p: idx(ι task[j],k ) = j.

div.head: III. A RECAP OF BASIC MULTI-RATE CYCLIC EXECUTIVES
div.p: For (basic) cyclic executives, tasks can simply be implemented as procedures and executed within a loop. A multirate cyclic executive essentially executes every task at least once in a cycle. In the following subsections, three basic types of multi-rate cyclic executives are recapitulated, AFAP, timedriven AFAP, and periodic.

div.head: A. Multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive

div.head: B. Multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: For a multi-rate time-driven AFAP, a cycle is started by a timer. The sum of the worst-case computation times of all jobs in a cycle shall be less than the inter-arrival time T S of the timer, otherwise the (worst-case) executions of the tasks do not 'fit' in a cycle, i.e.
div.formula: 1≤i≤n m i × WC i ≤ T S .
div.p: Figure 2 illustrates a multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive with cycle time T S , where the cycle is started at time Φ. By starting cycles with an inter-arrival time of T S , the spare time, i.e. the combination of slack time 1 and gain time 2 , can be used to execute background tasks or run the processor at a lower, more energy efficient, clock frequency after the cycle is completed.

div.head: C. Multi-rate periodic cyclic executive
div.p: For a multi-rate periodic cyclic executive, we focus on the 'strict' case, where every job is started at a specific time. In particular, for the 'strict' case we assume that every job is started at the worst-case start-time relative to the start of the cycle assuming each job needs its worst-case execution time.
Figure 3 illustrates such a multi-rate periodic cyclic executive with cycle time T S .

In a 'non-strict' case, not all tasks are necessarily started at a statically determined time, but some may be started immediately after the previous task completed. Hence, the multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive is a special case of a non-strict multi-rate periodic cyclic executive.

div.head: IV. EXACT ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we first recapitulate the general exact condition for the schedulability of a system S when tasks are scheduled by a basic cyclic executive. We subsequently present an example system, which we will use in the remainder of the section for illustration purposes. Next, we recapitulate the exact analysis for the multi-rate AFAP and multi-rate timedriven cyclic executive and present the exact analysis for the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive.

div.head: A. A recap of an exact schedulability condition
div.p: As described in [9], a system S meets its deadlines under a basic cyclic executive when the following schedulability condition holds
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∀ 0≤k f i,k+1 -s i,k ≤ WD S i ∧ BC i ≥ BD S i . (2)
div.p: The logical conjunction constituting this condition consists of two parts, a first part describing a worst-case schedulability condition, i.e. whether or not the system meets its worstcase deadlines, and a second part describing a best-case schedulability condition, i.e. whether or not a system meets its best-case deadlines.

The best-case schedulability condition is independent of a specific cyclic executive and checking the condition is considered trivial. We therefore focus on checking the worstcase schedulability condition.

Given the cyclic nature of the multi-rate cyclic executive and the fact that every task τ i is executed m i times in the cycle, it is sufficient to consider at most m i + 1, or m i pairs of, successive jobs of τ i . Hence, we can simplify the worstcase schedulability condition in (2) to
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∀ 0≤k≤mi-1 f i,k+1 -s i,k ≤ WD S i .
div.p: To determine whether or not system S meets all its worst-case deadlines, we therefore have to test at most N = 1≤i≤n m i conditions, where N reduces to n for the special case of singlerate executives, i.e. when ∀ 1≤i≤n m i = 1. From these m i pairs, m i -1 pairs are executed in the same cycle and 1 pair is executed in two successive cycles.

div.head: V. A COMPARISON OF BASIC CYCLIC EXECUTIVES
div.p: In this section, we discuss the relative strengths and weaknesses of the multi-rate cyclic executives considered.

div.head: A. Jitter
div.p: In this subsection, we focus on start jitter of tasks. 1) Multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive: As described in [7], a task τ i may experience unbounded start jitter or drift 3 under a multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive when 1≤j≤n BC j < 1≤j≤n WC j . 2) Multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive: As described in [7], a task τ i may experience (bounded) start jitter under a multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive.

3) Multi-rate periodic cyclic executive: Every job in a cycle has a fixed offset relative to the start of the cycle, e.g. the start time S i,k of jobι i,k with 1 ≤ i ≤ i and 0 ≤ k < m i relative to Φ is given by
div.formula: S i,k = 0≤ <idx(ι i,k ) WC task[ ] .
div.p: A task τ i is started strictly periodically when m i = 1. As illustrated for S I , a task τ i is not necessarily started strictly periodically whenever m i > 1, however. The fixed offset of jobs relative to the start of the cycle gives rise to limited start jitter compared to a multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive.

div.head: B. Energy efficiency
div.p: As described in [7], the multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive is energy inefficient, because the processor is constantly active executing tasks. Lemma 1 in [7] determines the fraction of time that can be gained for, for example, background processing by the multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive compared to the multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive. A proof for that lemma was not provided for reasons of lack of space. Below, we present a similar lemma for the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive, with a proof. Lemma 1. Whenever a system S with a sequence of tasks task[] is schedulable under a multi-rate periodic cyclic ex-ecutive with a cycle time of T S , a fraction f S,gain (T S ) given by

Proof. The term T S -1≤i≤n m i × WC i represents the worst-case (i.e. minimum) amount of spare time in a cycle and the term T S -1≤i≤n m i × BC i represents the bestcase (i.e. maximum) amount of spare time. The result therefore follows immediately.
In case of system S I and T SI = 12, we find 0 ≤ f SI,gain (12) ≤ 1 3 .

div.head: C. Schedulability
div.p: As already described by Theorem 3 in [7], the multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive dominates the multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. A proof of the theorem was omitted in [7] for reasons of lack of space. Below, we prove the theorem using an auxiliary lemma and our example system S I . We subsequently prove that the multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive and the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive can schedule the same systems. Finally, we prove that the multirate periodic cyclic executive also dominates the multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive.

div.head: D. Implementation overhead
div.p: The multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive has the lowest overhead of the three types of cyclic executives considered, i.e. only the execution of the while-loop contributes to the overhead. Unfortunately, the low overhead can not be exploited for other purposes.

The multi-rate periodic cyclic executive has the highest overhead, due to the additional for-loop, the additional N calculations of the value of time and the executions of the sleepuntil function; see Figure 3. Moreover, whenever the spare-time is used to run tasks in the background, that sparetime becomes available in a fragmented fashion, giving rise to additional context switches. As a result, for systems that (i) are schedulable by both the time-driven AFAP as well as the periodic cyclic executive, (ii) have similar values for the cycle time T S and (iii) are not sensitive to start jitter or finalization jitter, a multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive may therefore be preferred above a multi-rate periodic cyclic executive.

div.head: E. Summary
div.p: Table II briefly summarizes the comparison of the three basic multi-rate cyclic executives in this section. Based on this comparison, we draw the following conclusion:
1) periodic preferred above AFAP: Apart from having a higher overhead, the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive outperforms the multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive.

div.head: 2) periodic typically preferred above a time-driven AFAP:
div.p: Given the dominance of the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective, it is typically preferred above the multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. We used typically in our second conclusion, because the multirate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive may be preferred above the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive for specific cases; see Section V-D.

div.head: VI. DISCUSSION
div.p: In this section, we briefly discuss two options to partially lift the restriction of strictness.

div.head: A. 'Non-strict' multi-rate periodic cyclic executive
div.p: Considering Figure 4, we observe that both task τ 2 and τ 3 can be activated immediately after the completion of τ 1 without causing deadline misses; see Figure 5. In the resulting schedule, both task τ 2 and τ 3 have start jitter
div.formula: SJ 2 = SJ 3 = WC 1 -BC 1 = 1.
div.p: Selectively allowing jobs to start immediately after the completion of the previous job reduces the implementation overhead, albeit at the cost of an increase of the start jitter.

We finally observe that the so-called minor and major cycle, which are typically used to describe a (multi-rate) cyclic executive [5], do not apply for this example for two reasons. Firstly, the minor cycle and major cycle are generally taken to be the greatest common divisor (GCD) and the least common multiple (LCM) of the periods of the tasks, respectively. In our approach based on 'regularly polling tasks', we make no assumptions about periods (and deadlines) of tasks. Secondly, although the cycle time T SI may be viewed as the length of the major cycle, the minor cycle is not reflected in the example, due to the fact that task τ 1 is not activated strictly periodically, but with jitter.

div.head: B. 'Advanced strict' multi-rate periodic cyclic executive
div.p: Considering Figure 4, we observe that the 2 nd job of τ 1 in the cycle, i.e. job ι 1,1 , can be delayed with 1 time unit, resulting in an increase of T SI with 1 time unit, without causing deadline misses; see Figure 6. For the fraction f SI,gain , we now find for T SI = 13, 1 13 ≤ f SI,gain (13) ≤ 6 13 . In the resulting schedule, task τ 1 still has start-jitter, albeit less than in the original schedule, i.e. s 1,1s 1,0 = 6 < s 1,2s 1,1 = 7.

Selectively delaying jobs may further improve the energy efficiency of multi-rate periodic cyclic executives. Investigating such 'advanced strict' multi-rate periodic cyclic executives is a topic of future research.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we considered scheduling of independent polling tasks on a single processor using a multi-rate periodic cyclic executive. Unlike existing approaches, that take a 'software design' step by assuming periods and deadlines Fig. 6. A situation of worst-case execution for system S I under an 'advanced strict' multi-rate periodic cyclic executive using the sequence {1, 2, 1, 3} and a cycle time T S I = 13. All worst-case system deadlines of S I are met.

for tasks, we focussed on whether or not the deadlines of the system are met. We presented exact analysis for multi-rate periodic cyclic executives. Because best-case analysis turned out to be trivial, focus of this paper has been on exact worstcase analysis (Theorem 3). Our analysis derives feasible cycle times for a system. Next, we discussed the relative strengths and weaknesses of the multi-rate periodic cyclic executive compared to the multi-rate AFAP and multi-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, schedulability, and implementation overhead. In particular, we provided two schedulability related proofs. Firstly, we proved that the multi-rate AFAP cyclic executive and multirate periodic cyclic executive are equivalent from a scheduling perspective (Theorem 5). Secondly, we proved that the multirate periodic cyclic executives dominates the multi-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective (Theorem 6). Although the multi-rate periodic cyclic executives will typically be the preferred type of multi-rate cyclic executive, we identified specific cases where a multi-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executive may be preferred.

Investigating the 'non-strict' case of a multi-rate periodic cyclic executive, providing options to reduce both the implementation overhead and the fragmentation of spare time compared to the 'strict' case, is a topic of future work. Investigating 'advanced strict' cases, providing options to improve energy efficiency, is another topic. Other interesting directions for future work are refinements and extensions of the basic real-time system model, based on, e.g. the notion of observable event [11] or the single-path code paradigm [12].
